overview:
Honduras sits in the middle of Central America, with a long Caribbean coastline to the north and a short stretch of Pacific shore on the Gulf of Fonseca to the south. It borders Guatemala, El Salvador and Nicaragua and covers about 112,500 km², slightly larger than the US state of Tennessee. Around 10 million people live there, and the capital, Tegucigalpa, spreads across hills in the country's mountainous south.

Most Hondurans speak Spanish, while Garifuna, Miskito and English-speaking communities live along the Caribbean coast and on the Bay Islands. The ruins of Copán, a Maya city famous for its carved stone stairway, and the coral reefs around Roatán and Utila are the country's best-known treasures.

Honduras is a republic with an elected president. Coffee, bananas, palm oil and shrimp are big exports, and clothing factories employ many people. The country has struggled with poverty, hurricanes and crime, and many Hondurans have moved to the United States, sending money home that supports millions of families.
landAndNature:
Rugged mountains cover about three-quarters of Honduras, rising to Cerro Las Minas at about 2,870 meters. The Caribbean lowlands are hot and wet, dotted with banana plantations, while the vast, roadless rainforest of La Mosquitia in the east holds the Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve and the ruins of a lost city found by explorers in 2015. Pine forests cover the cooler highlands.

Offshore, the Bay Islands sit on the Mesoamerican Reef, the second-largest coral reef system in the world; whale sharks gather off Utila, and Roatán's reefs are crowded with divers. Scarlet macaws, the national bird, flash red over Copán, and jaguars, tapirs, howler monkeys and manatees live in the wild east. Hurricanes are a constant threat; Hurricane Mitch in 1998 killed thousands and destroyed much of the country's roads and bridges.
peopleAndCulture:
About nine in ten Hondurans are mestizo, of mixed Indigenous and Spanish descent, and Spanish is heard everywhere. The Lenca, Miskito and other Indigenous peoples keep their own traditions, and the Garifuna, descended from Africans and Caribbean islanders, are famous for punta drumming and dancing. Most people are Catholic or evangelical Christian.

The national snack is the baleada, a soft flour tortilla folded around beans, cheese and cream, sold at street stands everywhere. Tamales, fried fish with plantains, and coconut bread on the coast are other favorites. Soccer is the great passion, and the national team's matches bring the country to a standstill. La Ceiba's carnival in May is the biggest party of the year, and in Yoro people celebrate the Lluvia de Peces, when fish appear on the ground after heavy storms.
history:
The Maya city of Copán flourished between about 400 and 800 AD, ruled by a line of 16 kings who left behind exquisite stone portraits and the longest carved Maya text ever found. Christopher Columbus reached the mainland near Trujillo in 1502, and Spanish conquest followed; the Lenca chief Lempira led a fierce resistance in 1537 and the national currency is named after him.

Honduras became independent from Spain in 1821 and a separate republic in 1838. In the early 1900s US fruit companies came to dominate the economy, inspiring the term "banana republic." The country fought a short war with El Salvador in 1969. Military governments ruled for much of the century before elections resumed in 1982. Hurricane Mitch in 1998 and a coup in 2009 were major setbacks, and Honduras has worked since to strengthen its democracy.
funFacts: The name Honduras means "depths" in Spanish, said to come from Columbus's remark about the deep waters off the coast.
Copán's Hieroglyphic Stairway has about 2,000 carved glyphs, the longest known Maya inscription.
The term "banana republic" was coined in 1904 by the writer O. Henry in a story set in a fictional version of Honduras.
Whale sharks, the largest fish in the world, gather off the island of Utila almost year-round.
In the town of Yoro, small fish are found on the ground after storms in a yearly event locals call the Rain of Fish.
Honduras's national bird, the scarlet macaw, was revered by the ancient Maya at Copán, where it is still bred and released.
